item.title: Improper integrability and endpoint increments of weak piecewise future causal curves
item.statement: Let x:[a,b]->A, a<b, be a piecewise C^1 curve in the sense of def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline, with a finite partition a=s_0<...<s_m=b, C^1 on each open piece and finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of each piece. Assume its tangents are nonzero future causal at every open-piece point and at each one-sided endpoint. In any inertial chart write y=(y^0,z), z in R^3. On a piece (alpha,beta), choose r in (alpha,beta); for a function g continuous there, write integral_(alpha,beta) g for lim_(u downarrow alpha) integral_u^r g + lim_(v uparrow beta) integral_r^v g when both limits are finite. Then: (a) y is continuous on [alpha,beta], y^{0'}>=|z'|>=0 on (alpha,beta), and y^{0'}>0 there. (b) Every coordinate derivative is absolutely improperly Riemann integrable; its signed improper integral equals the corresponding endpoint increment. The continuous functions |z'| and f=sqrt((y^{0'})^2-|z'|^2)=sqrt(-eta(x',x')) have finite nonnegative improper integrals, with integral f<=integral y^{0'}=y^0(beta)-y^0(alpha). (c) The improper values are independent of r, additive under subdivision, and the finite piece sums are independent of the admissible partition. (d) D=x(b)-x(a) is nonzero future causal: D^0>0 and |D_spatial|<=D^0 in every inertial chart. If some interior or one-sided endpoint tangent is future timelike, D is future timelike. Coordinate time is strictly increasing on every nondegenerate subinterval. The integrals need not be ordinary closed-piece Riemann integrals. No derivative-limit hypothesis, Lebesgue-integration premise, clock identification, or choice principle is used.
item.strategy: Complete local adaptation of the flat future-cone integral argument, with endpoint integrability supplied rather than assumed. (a) Finite quotient derivative v at an endpoint gives x(t+h)-x(t)=h(v+o(1)), hence endpoint continuity; C1 gives interior continuity. The future cone coordinate criterion gives y0'>=|z'| and y0'>0 on each open piece. The square root is continuous on nonnegative reals: positive arguments use thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives with exponent 1/2; at zero, 0<=t<epsilon^2 implies 0<=sqrt(t)<epsilon. Thus the spatial norm and causal density are continuous even at a null tangent or a zero spatial component. Since y0'>=|z'|>=0, their squared values lie between 0 and (y0')^2, giving 0<=f<=y0' by the nonnegative square-root order. (b) On every alpha<u<v<beta, the derivative is continuous on [u,v], so thm-continuous-implies-integrable and thm-ftc-second-part give integral_u^v yj'=yj(v)-yj(u). Fix r inside. For y0' the left and right limits are y0(r)-y0(alpha) and y0(beta)-y0(r), finite by endpoint continuity and nonnegative. For any continuous 0<=g<=y0', the left truncation integrals are increasing as u decreases, bounded above by y0(r)-y0(alpha); completeness supplies their supremum S. Given epsilon>0 choose u* with integral_u*^r g>S-epsilon; every alpha<u<u* then has integral_u^r g between S-epsilon and S, proving the limit S. The right side is identical. Apply this to |yj'|, |z'| and f; all are continuous inside and bounded above by y0'. Signed coordinate integrals converge by the truncated FTC and endpoint continuity; thus each derivative is absolutely improperly integrable and has the exact endpoint increment. (c) Ordinary integral additivity on truncations and finite limits show independence of r and additivity under each interior cut. Any two admissible finite partitions have a common refinement, so all finite sums agree. (d) On truncations, the vector-integral norm inequality gives |z(v)-z(u)|<=integral_u^v |z'|<=integral_u^v y0'. Pass to endpoints and sum with the Euclidean triangle inequality to obtain |D_spatial|<=D0. Positive y0' on a compact interior interval gives a positive time increment, and nonnegativity on the rest gives D0>0; apply the same argument to any nondegenerate restriction for strict time monotonicity. At an interior timelike tangent, y0'-|z'| is continuous and positive in a compact interior neighborhood, so its integral is positive and the inequality becomes strict. At a left endpoint with timelike one-sided quotient v, (y(alpha+h)-y(alpha))/h tends to v, so for some h>0 that quotient is future timelike by openness of the cone. This subdisplacement is future timelike, and the remaining subdisplacement is future causal by the already proved non-strict inequality; adding their coordinates yields a future timelike sum. At a right endpoint use (y(beta)-y(beta-h))/h similarly. At a corner use the corresponding adjacent piece. This proves the endpoint-only timelike clause without continuity of the derivative at the corner. No closed-piece derivative integrability or countable choice is assumed.

item.title: Proper time is invariant under regular increasing weak piecewise changes of parameter
item.statement: Let c>0 and let x:[a,b]->A be a weak piecewise C^1 future timelike worldline. Let phi:[u,v]->[a,b] be an increasing continuous surjection, C^1 on the open pieces of a finite partition, with phi'>0 at every interior smooth point and finite positive one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both endpoints of each piece. Then phi is strictly increasing with continuous inverse, y=x composed with phi is a weak piecewise C^1 future timelike worldline, and Delta tau_[u,v](y)=Delta tau_[a,b](x). The same equality holds for every pair of corresponding restricted parameter intervals; based proper-time functions differ only by their base-point constant. The relevant partition is the common refinement of phi's partition and the inverse images of x's partition points. This statement gives worldline/clock consequences only for positive derivatives, including all one-sided endpoint derivatives. It leaves intact the separate global-C^1 curve-integral identities allowing zero tangents in lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance; a zero-tangent composition is not asserted to be a worldline.
item.strategy: On each closed piece phi is continuous and differentiable inside with phi'>0, so the mean value theorem proves strict increase there; finite concatenation gives global strict increase, and the continuous monotone bijection has continuous inverse. The finite inverse-image refinement separates all x and phi corners. Inside each refined piece componentwise chain rule gives y'=phi' x'(phi), so y' is continuous and future timelike and sqrt(-eta(y',y'))=phi' f(phi), where f=sqrt(-eta(x',x')). At each one-sided endpoint the quotient of y is the product of the corresponding quotient of x and that of phi; strict monotonicity chooses the correct side and both finite limits exist, the latter positive. Thus y has finite future timelike one-sided tangents and lies in the same weak class. On any compact interior truncation [r,s] of a refined piece, f is continuous on the compact image interval and phi' is continuous and integrable on [r,s]; thm-substitution gives integral_r^s phi' f(phi)=integral_phi(r)^phi(s) f. As r and s approach the refined endpoints, continuity and strict monotonicity of phi make the image endpoints approach the corresponding x endpoints. Both improper limits exist by lem-sr-weak-piecewise-causal-integrability for x and y, so the identity passes to the limits. Finite summation and partition independence give the full and restricted interval identities. Oriented additivity gives the based-function constant. No boundedness of the derivative near a corner is assumed and no zero tangent is admitted as a worldline.

before.title: Distributional continuity of a moving point charge
before.statement: Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ with graph contained in an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, and let $q\in\mathbb R$. For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ define $$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle:=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,\qquad \langle J,\psi\rangle:=q\int_Iz'(t)\,\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,$$ the integrands having compact support in $I$. Then $\rho,J\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$.
before.strategy: Pair the divergence with a test: $-q\int_I[\partial_t\psi(z(t),t)+z'(t)\cdot\nabla\psi(z(t),t)]\,dt=-q\int_I\frac{d}{dt}\psi(z(t),t)\,dt=0$, since $t\mapsto\psi(z(t),t)$ is $C^1$ with compact support. The chain rule supplies the derivative. Only prescribed point support is proved; Maxwell existence and point self-force are not asserted.

after.title: Distributional continuity of a moving point charge
after.statement: Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$ a $C^1$ trajectory, and $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ open containing its graph. Assume the graph map $\gamma:I\to\Omega$, $\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$, is proper: the inverse image of every compact subset of $\Omega$ is compact in $I$. For $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ define $\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$ and $\langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_I z'(t)\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$. These define distributions and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. Properness is automatic if $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, or if $I=\mathbb R$. Endpoint variant: if $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, the absolute improper integral $\int_a^b|z'(t)|\,dt$ is finite, and both endpoint events belong to $\Omega$, the same integrals instead define distributions with $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\delta_{(z(a),a)}-q\delta_{(z(b),b)}$. A finite-history source is source-free only when the endpoint contribution vanishes on the chosen test domain; neither mere graph containment nor test compactness alone supplies this.
after.strategy: For a fixed compact test support $K\subset\Omega$, properness makes $\gamma^{-1}(K)$ compact in $I$. It lies in one closed interior interval $[u,v]\subset I$, on which $z'$ is bounded. Both pairings are bounded by constants depending on $K$ times $\sup_K|\psi|$, proving distribution continuity on each test-support space. The pullback of a test is $C^1$ and compactly supported in $I$. By the total chain rule, pairing the divergence gives $-q\int_I[\partial_t\psi(z(t),t)+z'(t)\cdot\nabla\psi(z(t),t)]dt=-q\int_I(d/dt)\psi(z(t),t)dt=0$ by interior FTC. For $I=\mathbb R$, compact ambient support bounds the time coordinate and its graph preimage is a closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R$; for $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, compact ambient support has time projection compact inside $I$. This proves both automatic properness claims. In the endpoint variant, finite interval length and the finite absolute improper integral of $z'$ bound the pairings on every compact test support. Apply the chain rule and FTC on $[a+\epsilon,b-\epsilon]$; the derivative pullback is absolutely integrable, and continuity at endpoints gives the limiting identity $q\psi(z(a),a)-q\psi(z(b),b)$. This proves the two endpoint deltas. In particular $I=(0,1),z=0,\Omega=\mathbb R^4$ gives $q\delta_{(0,0)}-q\delta_{(0,1)}$, refuting the old unconditional claim. The endpoint integration limit is explicitly this truncation argument, not an invented source reading. Maxwell existence and point self-force are not asserted. Here the two-ended improper integral means the sum of the limits of integrals on [a+epsilon,r] and [r,b−epsilon] for any fixed interior r. Monotonicity and completeness prove convergence of every nonnegative integrand bounded by a constant times 1+|z′|; signed limits then follow from the positive and negative parts. Thus the endpoint variant uses only the explicitly supplied improper convention and truncated ordinary FTC.

before.title: Global existence, uniqueness and differentiability of the retarded root
before.statement:
Let $c>0$, let $v_*<c$, and let $z:\mathbb R	o\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) with $|z'(t)|\le v_*$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$; let $x\in\mathbb R^3$ be a point with $x
e z(t)$ for all $t$. For every $t\in\mathbb R$ there is exactly one $s<t$ with $$t-s=|x-z(s)|/c .$$ On the open set of pairs $(x,t)$ with $x
e z(t)$ the root map $s(x,t)$ is of class $C^3$, and its derivatives are $$\partial_ts(x,t)=\kappa^{-1},\qquad 
abla_xs(x,t)=- rac{n}{c\,\kappa},\qquad \kappa=1-n\cdot eta,\quad n= rac{x-z(s)}{|x-z(s)|},\  eta= rac{z'(s)}{c},$$ with $\kappa\in[1-v_*/c,\,1+v_*/c]$ uniformly bounded below by $1-v_*/c>0$. Nothing is asserted for a finite-history trajectory, for a trajectory whose speed approaches $c$ without a uniform bound, or about the complete retarded field formula of the causal-response page.
before.strategy: Define $f(s)=t-s-|x-z(s)|/c$ on $\mathbb R$ (for the fixed pair $(x,t)$). It is continuous, $f(t)<0$ because $x\ne z(t)$, and $|z(s)|\le|z(0)|+v_*|s|$ makes $f(s)\to+\infty$ as $s\to-\infty$. For $s_2>s_1$ the integral representation of $z(s_2)-z(s_1)$ together with the integral triangle inequality ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) gives $|z(s_2)-z(s_1)|\le v_*(s_2-s_1)$, hence $f(s_2)-f(s_1)\le-(1-v_*/c)(s_2-s_1)<0$: $f$ is strictly decreasing. The intermediate value theorem ([[thm-intermediate-value]]) and strict decrease give one root, strictly below $t$. At that root $r=c(t-s)>0$, so $|x-z(\cdot)|$ is a composition of smooth maps on a neighbourhood of $s$ and $\partial_sf=-\kappa\le-(1-v_*/c)<0$ is bounded away from zero uniformly. The parametrized implicit function theorem with $C^k$ regularity ([[thm-parametrized-implicit-function-theorem-with-higher-regularity]]) applied to $F(x,t,s)=t-s-|x-z(s)|/c$ gives $C^3$ regularity of $s(x,t)$ and the derivative formula $Ds=-F_s^{-1}D_{(x,t)}F$; differentiating $f=0$ gives $\partial_ts=\kappa^{-1}$ and $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$.

after.title: Global existence, uniqueness and differentiability of the retarded root
after.statement: Let $c>0$, $0\le v_*<c$, and $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for all $s$. For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ there is exactly one real root $s=s(x,t)$ of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and $s\le t$. Equality holds exactly when $x=z(t)$. Thus on the open off-instantaneous-worldline domain $D=\{(x,t):x\ne z(t)\}$ one has $s<t$, $r=|x-z(s)|=c(t-s)>0$, and the root is $C^1$. With $n=(x-z(s))/r$, $\beta=z'(s)/c$, and $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$, its derivatives are $\partial_t s=1/\kappa$ and $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$, where $1-v_*/c\le\kappa\le1+v_*/c$. If $z$ is $C^k$, for an integer $k\ge1$, the root is $C^k$ on $D$; in particular a $C^3$ trajectory gives a $C^3$ root. A smooth trajectory gives a smooth root. No higher regularity follows from a merely $C^1$ trajectory. These claims concern an all-time uniformly subluminal prescribed history; no finite-history or nonuniform-light-speed-limit assertion is made.
after.strategy: The ordinary vector FTC and integral triangle inequality give $|z(s_2)-z(s_1)|\le v_*|s_2-s_1|$. For fixed $x$ put $g_x(s)=s+|x-z(s)|/c$. It is continuous and for $s_2>s_1$ satisfies $g_x(s_2)-g_x(s_1)\ge(1-v_*/c)(s_2-s_1)>0$. Consequently $g_x(s)\to\pm\infty$ as $s\to\pm\infty$; IVT and strict monotonicity give a unique solution of $g_x(s)=t$. Since $g_x(s)\ge s$, $s\le t$, and equality is equivalent to $x=z(t)$. On $D$ the root has $r>0$. Continuity of $z$ makes $D$ open. Near any root on $D$, $F(x,t,s)=t-s-|x-z(s)|/c$ has precisely the regularity of $z$, because the Euclidean norm is smooth away from zero. Its $s$ derivative is $-\kappa$, bounded away from zero. Apply the parametrized implicit-function theorem with its actual $C^1$ hypothesis first, or with $C^k$ when $z$ is $C^k$; global uniqueness glues these local maps. Differentiating $F=0$ gives the two stated formulas. Repeat for every finite $k$ in the smooth case. Do not infer $C^3$ from $C^1$, and do not exclude an observation point merely because the trajectory visits it at a different time. The exact non-improvement witness is a small uniformly subluminal $z(s)=(\epsilon\chi(s)|s|^{3/2},0,0)$ with smooth compact cutoff $\chi=1$ near zero. At a distant positive axial point $L>\sup|z|$, the retardation map is $g(s)=s+(L-\epsilon\chi(s)|s|^{3/2})/c$, $C^1$ but not $C^2$ at zero. A $C^2$ inverse near $t=L/c$, whose derivative is nonzero, would make $g$ $C^2$ by the inverse-function theorem, a contradiction.

before.title: Dispersion relations for an absolutely continuous integrable causal kernel
before.statement: Let $d\ge1$ and let $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be a locally absolutely continuous matrix kernel with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ (entrywise integrability), and let $$\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds\qquad(\operatorname{Im}z>0)$$ be the matrix response function. Then the entries of $\chi$ are holomorphic functions on the upper half-plane ([[def-complex-domain]]), continuous and $C^1$ on its real boundary, bounded on the closed upper half-plane with $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K'_{jk}\|_1$ for $|z|\ge1$, and the entrywise principal-value dispersion formulas hold: for real $\omega$, $$\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi .$$ An instantaneous real response matrix may be added as $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$, in which case the formulas apply to $\chi-\chi_\infty$; the scalar case is $d=1$. Causality alone supplies neither growth assumptions beyond those stated nor the passivity quadratic-form condition, which is a separate model assertion.
before.strategy: Absolute integrability bounds each entry of $\chi$ on the closed upper half-plane, and continuity is by dominated convergence ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). For $\operatorname{Im}z\ge\delta>0$ the parameter derivatives have the integrable entrywise bound $|s\,e^{izs}|\le s\,e^{-\delta s}$, so differentiation under the integral sign ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]) gives holomorphy of each entry; the hypothesis $sK\in L^1$ makes the entrywise first derivative continuous on the real boundary. Local absolute continuity with $K'\in L^1$ and $K\in L^1$ gives $K(s)\to0$ at infinity (as a matrix), and entrywise integration by parts ([[thm-integration-by-parts]]) gives $\chi(z)=-K(0)/(iz)-(iz)^{-1}\int_0^\infty K'(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ for $z\ne0$, hence the uniform entrywise bound $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le[|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K'_{jk}\|_1]/|z|$. Apply Cauchy's theorem for null-homotopic loops ([[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]], with complex line integrals along closed rectifiable contours, [[thm-existence-of-complex-line-integrals-on-rectifiable-paths]]) to each entry of $\chi(z)/(z-\omega)$ on the indented upper-semicircle domain (a small semicircular indentation around the real point $\omega$ and a large half-circle of radius $R$). The large-arc integrand is $O(R^{-2})$ on length $\pi R$ and tends to zero; the indentation contributes $-i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)$; separating the remaining real-axis principal values gives the displayed pair of formulas entrywise, the $O(|\xi|^{-1})+C^1$ control of the tail ensuring the principal values exist. The matrix form reduces to the scalar form in each entry, and $\chi_\infty$ is handled by subtracting it before the contour argument.

after.title: Dispersion relations for an absolutely continuous integrable causal kernel
after.statement: Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $d\ge1$ and let $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be a locally absolutely continuous matrix kernel with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ (entrywise integrability), and let $$\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds\qquad(\operatorname{Im}z>0)$$ be the matrix response function. Here locally absolutely continuous means that each real entry restricted to every compact interval $[a,b]\subseteq[0,\infty)$ satisfies the finite disjoint-interval condition of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]: for every $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $\sum_\ell(v_\ell-u_\ell)<\delta$ implies $\sum_\ell|K_{jk}(v_\ell)-K_{jk}(u_\ell)|<\epsilon$ for every finite family with disjoint interiors. $K\prime$ denotes the almost-everywhere derivative, with any measurable zero extension on its null exceptional set. Then the entries of $\chi$ are holomorphic functions on the upper half-plane ([[def-complex-domain]]), continuous and $C^1$ on its real boundary, bounded on the closed upper half-plane with $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K'_{jk}\|_1$ for $|z|\ge1$, and the entrywise principal-value dispersion formulas hold: for real $\omega$, $$\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi .$$ The sharper bound $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le(|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K\prime_{jk}\|_1)/|z|$ holds for every nonzero $z$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$. Here $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi$ means $\lim_{R\to\infty}\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}(\int_{\omega-R}^{\omega-\eta}+\int_{\omega+\eta}^{\omega+R})F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi$; the tails converge absolutely, so the choice of centering at infinity does not change the limit. For an instantaneous real response matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ define the total transfer function $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}:=\chi_\infty+\chi$; the formulas then apply to $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty=\chi$; the scalar case is $d=1$. Causality alone supplies neither growth assumptions beyond those stated nor the passivity quadratic-form condition, which is a separate model assertion.
after.strategy:
Treat each real entry $k=K_{jk}$ separately. Its locally absolutely continuous representative is the one in the statement; the published [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] applies on $[0,N]$ under the declared Countable Choice and Dependent Choice and yields $k(s)=k(0)+\int_0^s k\prime(u)du$. Since $k\prime\in L^1$, dominated convergence shows this has a finite limit $\ell=k(0)+\int_0^\infty k\prime$. If $\ell\ne0$, then $|k(s)|\ge|\ell|/2$ for all sufficiently large $s$, contradicting $k\in L^1$ by monotonicity of the integral ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Hence $k(s)\to0$.
The defining integral is bounded by $\|k\|_1$ on $\overline H$, and dominated convergence gives joint continuity there ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). Writing $z=x+iy$, the real parameter derivatives of $k(s)e^{izs}$ are $isk(s)e^{izs}$ and $-sk(s)e^{izs}$. On any rectangle in $H$ their absolute values are bounded by $s|k(s)|$, integrable by hypothesis. [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] applied separately in $x,y$ supplies the partials; dominated convergence makes them continuous, and $\partial_y\chi=i\partial_x\chi$ gives holomorphy by [[thm-continuous-partials-and-cauchy-riemann-imply-holomorphic]]. Along the real boundary the same theorem in the real parameter and the same majorant give the continuous derivative $\chi\prime(\omega)=\int_0^\infty isk(s)e^{i\omega s}ds$.
For fixed $z\ne0$, the real and imaginary parts of $g(s):=e^{izs}$ are $C^1$ on each $[0,N]$, hence absolutely continuous by [[thm-c1-lipschitz-ac-bv-hierarchy]]. Apply [[thm-integration-by-parts-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] separately to $(k,\operatorname{Re}g)$ and $(k,\operatorname{Im}g)$ and combine the real identities to get
$$\int_0^N k(s)e^{izs}ds=\frac{k(N)e^{izN}-k(0)}{iz}-\frac1{iz}\int_0^N k\prime(s)e^{izs}ds.$$
This is Lebesgue integration by parts for AC functions, not the ordinary everywhere-differentiable Riemann theorem. For $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, $|e^{izs}|\le1$; $k(N)\to0$ kills the endpoint term and dominated convergence applies to both integrals. Thus
$$\chi_{jk}(z)=-\frac{k(0)}{iz}-\frac1{iz}\int_0^\infty k\prime(s)e^{izs}ds,\qquad |\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\frac{|k(0)|+\|k\prime\|_1}{|z|}.$$
For completeness the boundary contour step is valid for any scalar $F$ holomorphic on $H:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on $\overline H$, with $C^1$ real boundary restriction and $F(z)=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly on $\overline H$ at infinity. Fix $\omega\in\mathbb R$, $R>|\omega|+2$ and $0<\eta<1$. Use the real intervals from $\omega-R$ to $\omega-\eta$ and $\omega+\eta$ to $\omega+R$, a clockwise upper semicircle of radius $\eta$ about $\omega$, and the counterclockwise large upper semicircle of radius $R$ about $\omega$. For $\delta>0$ apply [[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]] to $F(z+i\delta)/(z-\omega)$ on $D_\delta:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>-\delta/2\}\setminus\{\omega-iv:v\ge0\}$. This open domain is star-shaped about any point $\omega+iA$, $A>0$, so the contour is null-homotopic there and the integrand is holomorphic. All contour pieces lie in $D_\delta$; no analytic extension of $F$ across the real boundary is assumed. before.statement: Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $\omega_0\in\mathbb R$, and let $\chi$ be holomorphic on the upper half-plane, of class $C^1$ on its real boundary away from $\omega_0$, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\omega_0$ in $\mathbb C$, and satisfying $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ on $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ outside a compact set ([[def-complex-domain]]). before.title: Causal convolution response, transfer function and dispersion relations
before.reference: completed-expansion-arguments.md#D1-D2 (compact and W^{1,1} integrable causal branches), assembled with the passivity quadratic form
before.statement:
Let $d\ge1$. All kernels below are real $d\times d$ matrix kernels and all histories are $\mathbb R^d$-valued; conditions on matrices are read entrywise, and $L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ means entrywise Lebesgue integrability on $(0,\infty)$.

(a) (Causal convolution.) Let $K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and let $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and continuous. Then for every $t\in\mathbb R$ the integral $P(t):=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ converges absolutely, $$|P_j(t)|\le\sum_{k=1}^d\Bigl(\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}|E_k(s)|\Bigr)\int_0^\infty|K_{jk}(s)|\,ds\qquad(j=1,\dots,d),$$ the response $P$ is bounded and continuous, the map $E\mapsto P$ is linear, and it is causal: if $E_1,E_2$ are bounded continuous and coincide on $(-\infty,t_0]$, then their responses coincide on $(-\infty,t_0]$.

(b) (Compact branch.) If $K\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ (smooth, with compact support contained in the open half-line), then the transfer function $$\chi(z):=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$$ is entire, satisfies $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for every real $\omega$, obeys $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\|K_{jk}''\|_{L^1(0,\infty)}|z|^{-2}$ for every $z\ne0$, and its entries satisfy the principal-value dispersion relations $$\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi$$ for every real $\omega$.

(c) (Integrable branch.) If instead $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is locally absolutely continuous (absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of $[0,\infty)$) with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $s\mapsto sK(s)$ in $L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$, then $\chi(z):=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ is well defined and holomorphic on the open upper half-plane $\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on the closed upper half-plane with continuous first derivative on the real boundary, satisfies the same pair of dispersion relations for every real $\omega$, and is bounded on $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge0\}$ by $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K_{jk}'\|_{L^1(0,\infty)}$ for $|z|\ge1$; for an instantaneous real response matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ the relations hold with $\chi$ replaced by $\chi-\chi_\infty$.

(d) (Monochromatic work and passivity.) Let $\omega>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^d$, and let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be a real parameter (a response normalization; the equivalence below is independent of its value). Put $E(t):=\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{-i\omega t})$ and $P(t):=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\,e^{-i\omega t})$, real parts taken componentwise and $\chi(\omega)$ acting by matrix multiplication. Then, with $T:=2\pi/\omega$ and the Euclidean dot product on $\mathbb R^d$, $$\frac1T\int_0^T E(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e\bigr),\qquad e^*\chi(\omega)e:=\sum_{j,k=1}^d\overline{e_j}\,\chi_{jk}(\omega)\,e_k,$$ and this period-averaged work is nonnegative for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$ if and only if the Hermitian part $M(\omega):=(\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*)/(2i)$ satisfies $e^*M(\omega)e\ge0$ for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$.
before.strategy:
Proof technique: direct, branch by branch; clausal tags below indicate the cited tools.

(a) For each $j$ and $t$, absolute convergence and the displayed bound follow from $|K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)|\le(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}(s)|$, the triangle inequality for integrals and monotonicity of the nonnegative integral over the measurable set $(0,\infty)$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]). Linearity in $E$ is linearity of the integral. Continuity in $t$: if $t_n\to t$ then $K_{jk}(s)E_k(t_n-s)\to K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)$ for every $s$ with the integrable dominating function $(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}|$, so dominated convergence gives $P(t_n)\to P(t)$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). Causality: for $t\le t_0$ and every $s\ge0$ the argument $t-s$ lies in $(-\infty,t_0]$, so replacing $E$ by a history agreeing with it there changes no integrand value and hence no integral.

(b) Holomorphy is obtained from the real-parameter differentiation theorem rather than by differentiating in the complex variable directly. Writing $z=x+iy$, the integrand $K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}=K_{jk}(s)e^{ixs}e^{-ys}$ has continuous partials in $x$ and $y$; because $K_{jk}$ has compact support, on every compact set of parameters $(x,y)$ the partials are dominated by a fixed multiple of $|K_{jk}|(1+|s|)$, an integrable function, so [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] applied in the two real parameters gives the continuous partials $\partial_x\chi_{jk}=\int_0^\infty isK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ and $\partial_y\chi_{jk}=\int_0^\infty(-s)K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). These satisfy $\partial_y\chi_{jk}=-\int sK_{jk}e^{izs}=i\int isK_{jk}e^{izs}=i\,\partial_x\chi_{jk}$, the Cauchy--Riemann equations for the pair $(\partial_x\chi_{jk},\partial_y\chi_{jk})$ with the identification $f=u+iv$; since the partials exist on a neighbourhood and are continuous, [[thm-continuous-partials-and-cauchy-riemann-imply-holomorphic]] makes $\chi_{jk}$ holomorphic, and because the same argument is available at every $z\in\mathbb C$, each entry is entire ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]). Iterating gives $\chi_{jk}^{(k)}(z)=\int_0^\infty(is)^kK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$. For the reality identity at real $\omega$: conjugation is an isometry and a real-field automorphism of $\mathbb C$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]) and the series defining the complex exponential converges everywhere ([[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]); conjugating the partial sums termwise and passing to the limit along the isometry gives $\overline{e^{i\omega s}}=e^{-i\omega s}$, so conjugating the defining integral of $\chi_{jk}$ and using that $K_{jk}$ is real gives $\overline{\chi_{jk}(\omega)}=\int_0^\infty K_{jk}(s)e^{-i\omega s}\,ds=\chi_{jk}(-\omega)$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). Two integrations by parts with vanishing endpoint values, valid because $K$ vanishes near $0$ and at infinity, give $\chi_{jk}(z)=-z^{-2}\int_0^\infty K_{jk}''(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ for $z\ne0$, hence the stated $|z|^{-2}$ bound ([[thm-integration-by-parts]]). For the dispersion relations fix real $\omega$ and form a contour consisting of the interval $[-R,R]$ indented above $\omega$ on a clockwise semicircle of radius $\delta$, closed by the large semicircle of radius $R$ in the upper half-plane; on the indented domain the integrand $\chi_{jk}(z)/(z-\omega)$ is holomorphic, so Cauchy's theorem for null-homotopic loops gives vanishing total integral ([[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]]). The large arc contributes at most $\pi R\sup_{|z|=R}|\chi_{jk}|/R\to0$ by the $|z|^{-2}$ bound. The small arc contributes $-i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)+o(1)$ as $\delta\to0$, by continuity of $\chi_{jk}$ on the closed upper half-plane, which follows from dominated convergence as in (a) ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). The remaining real integral converges to its principal value: near $\omega$ subtract the constant $\chi_{jk}(\omega)$ so that the divided difference $[\chi_{jk}(\xi)-\chi_{jk}(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded, and at infinity use the $|z|^{-2}$ decay. Letting $\delta\to0$, $R\to\infty$ gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\chi_{jk}(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)$; separating real and imaginary parts yields the displayed pair because $i(a+ib)=-b+ia$.

(c) This is precisely the content of the cited integrable-causal-dispersion lemma: that item proves, under exactly these hypotheses, the holomorphy on the upper half-plane ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]), the closed-half-plane bound, the boundary regularity and the two principal-value formulas, and records the instantaneous-response subtraction ([[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]]). The present theorem assembles the response, its transfer function and the passivity relation around that lemma; no additional proof obligation is created here.

(d) The period-average of a product of real parts of complex exponentials is supplied by [[lem-em-period-average]], which states exactly $\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})dt=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(a\cdot\overline d)$; applying it with $a=e$ and $d=(-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e$ (the derivative of $t\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\,e^{-i\omega t})$, computed with the chain rule) gives $$\frac1T\int_0^TE(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\Bigl(e\cdot\overline{(-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e}\Bigr)=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e\bigr),$$ using $e\cdot\overline{\chi(\omega)e}=\overline{e^*\chi(\omega)e}$ and $\operatorname{Re}(-iz)=\operatorname{Im}z$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]). Finally $e^*M(\omega)e=(e^*\chi(\omega)e-e^*\chi(\omega)^*e)/(2i)=\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi(\omega)e)$ because $M(\omega)$ is the Hermitian part of $\chi(\omega)$, so nonnegativity of the displayed average for every $e$ is exactly the stated quadratic-form condition. The logical independence of causality and this positivity (the design's 'no sign of dissipation follows merely from causality') is exhibited on the companion example page by a kernel satisfying (c) whose quadratic form is strictly negative.

The remaining real integral converges to its principal value: near $\omega$ subtract the constant $\chi_{jk}(\omega)$ so that the divided difference $[\chi_{jk}(\xi)-\chi_{jk}(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded, and at infinity use the $|z|^{-2}$ decay. before.title: Hypothesis boundaries: a causal response without passivity, and the fixed-retarded-time flux limit
before.reference: mathematical-example-verifications.md#ex-em-causal-response-and-radiation-prerequisites-hypothesis-boundaries; clause (ii) added by this scaffolder to exercise the second theorem's declared dependency (recorded in the batch notes)
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the surface-integral conventions used by [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]].

(i) (Causality without passivity.) Let $K(s):=-e^{-s}$ for $s\ge0$. Then $K$ is of class $C^1$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty)$ and $sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty)$ (indeed $K'=e^{-s}=-K$, $\int_0^\infty e^{-s}ds=1$ and $\int_0^\infty se^{-s}ds=1$), so the integrable branch of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]] applies: $P(t)=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)ds$ is a bounded causal linear response on bounded continuous histories, its transfer function is $\chi(z)=-1/(1-iz)$ on $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, and its boundary value $\chi(\omega)=-(1+i\omega)/(1+\omega^2)$ satisfies $\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=-\omega/(1+\omega^2)<0$ for every $\omega>0$. Hence the Hermitian part $M(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)$ is strictly negative, not positive semidefinite, and the monochromatic period-averaged work of clause (d) of that theorem is strictly negative for $d=1$, every $e\ne0$ and every $\omega>0$ (with any response normalization $\varepsilon_0>0$), although the response is causal and its entry satisfies the dispersion relations of clause (c). Nonnegative period-averaged work (passivity) is therefore an additional condition on the model, not a consequence of temporal causality.

(ii) (The flux limit needs fixed retarded time.) In the setting of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]], fix $t\in\mathbb R$ and $n\in S^2$, and let $r>\max\{2a,\;a+c(t-t_0)\}$. Then for every $y\in B_a$ one has $R=|rn-y|\ge r-a>c(t-t_0)$, so $t-R/c<t_0$; by hypothesis (H1) of that theorem the functions $\rho,\rho_t,\mathbf J,\mathbf J_t$ all vanish at $(y,t-R/c)$, so every integrand in the field formulas of clause (a) of that theorem vanishes and $\mathbf E(rn,t)=\mathbf B(rn,t)=0$, hence $n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)=0$ for every $n\in S^2$. Therefore $\int_{S^2}r^2\,n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)\,d\Omega(n)=0$ for all such $r$: at fixed observation time the far-zone flux integral is identically zero beyond the light cone of the compact spacetime support, whereas clause (c) of that theorem is a limit at fixed retarded time. The retarded-time formulation cannot be replaced by a fixed-observation-time one.

Proof technique: direct computation and direct substitution into the two cited theorems.

(i) The real exponential is differentiable with $\exp'=\exp$ ([[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]) and $\exp(-s)>0$ with $\exp(-s)=1/\exp(s)$ ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]), so $s\mapsto K(s)=-e^{-s}$ is of class $C^1$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $K'=e^{-s}=-K$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). For every $N>0$ the Newton-Leibniz formula gives $\int_0^Ne^{-s}ds=1-e^{-N}$ and integration by parts (with $u=s$, $v=-e^{-s}$) gives $\int_0^Nse^{-s}ds=1-(1+N)e^{-N}$ ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]], [[thm-integration-by-parts]]); these integral representations over compact intervals are the absolute-continuity property required by the integrable branch of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]], and passing to the limit with monotone convergence for the nonnegative integrands gives $\int_0^\infty e^{-s}ds=\int_0^\infty se^{-s}ds=1$, so $K,K',sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty)$ ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]). Clause (a) of the theorem therefore gives the bounded causal response. For the transfer function, fix real $\omega$; the complex exponential is entire with derivative itself and the complex chain rule gives that $s\mapsto F(s)=\exp((-1+i\omega)s)/(-1+i\omega)$ is a primitive of $s\mapsto\exp((-1+i\omega)s)$ on $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]], [[def-complex-exponential]]), so the fundamental theorem for complex line integrals along the interval path $[0,N]\ni s\mapsto s$ gives $\int_{[0,N]}\exp((-1+i\omega)s)\,ds=F(N)-F(0)$ ([[thm-fundamental-theorem-for-complex-line-integrals]], [[def-complex-primitive]], [[def-complex-line-integral-over-a-rectifiable-path]], [[thm-riemann-stieltjes-and-parametric-contour-integrals-agree]]). Hence $\int_0^N(-e^{-s})e^{i\omega s}ds=-(F(N)-F(0))$, and $\left|e^{(-1+i\omega)N}\right|=e^{-N}\to0$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]); letting $N\to\infty$ with dominated convergence for the integrands dominated by $e^{-s}$ gives $\chi(\omega)=-1/(1-i\omega)$, and the same computation with $z$ in place of $\omega$ gives $\chi(z)=-1/(1-iz)$ for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). Taking real and imaginary parts ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) gives $\chi(\omega)=-(1+i\omega)/(1+\omega^2)$ and $\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=-\omega/(1+\omega^2)<0$ because $\omega>0$. (ii) For $y\in B_a$ the reverse triangle inequality gives $R=|rn-y|\ge r-a>c(t-t_0)$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), hence $t-R/c<t_0$ and all four source functions vanish at the arguments appearing in the field integrals of clause (a) of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]]; each integrand is identically zero on $B_a$, so $\mathbf E(rn,t)=\mathbf B(rn,t)=0$ and therefore $n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)=\mu_0^{-1}n\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)(rn,t)=0$ for every $n\in S^2$. before.statement: Let $c>0$, $q\in\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, put $\mu_0:=(c^2\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ and $C:=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*<c$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Write $\Omega:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and $\Gamma:=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}\subseteq\Omega$. For $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ let $s=s(x,t)$ be the unique retarded root of [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]] with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and put $R:=x-z(s)$, $r:=|R|>0$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s)/c$, $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$, $N:=n\cdot\beta$, $D:=\kappa r$, $\dot\beta:=z''(s)/c$ and $d:=n\cdot\dot\beta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then: (a) the distributions $\rho,J\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]], $$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad \langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)\,\psi(z(s),s)\,ds,$$ satisfy $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. (b) Let $K$ be the retarded wave kernel of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] and, for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and $\tau\in\mathbb R$, $y\in\mathbb R^3$, put $(K\circledast\psi)(y,\tau):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,\tau+\cdot)\rangle$. Then the pairings $$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle:=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\langle\rho,K\circledast\psi\rangle=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R}(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle:=\mu_0\langle J,K\circledast\psi\rangle$$ are finite for every $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and satisfy the exact retarded-convolution identities $$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{\beta(x,t)}{c}\,\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt$$ (for $\Upsilon$, componentwise against $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$; both integrands are continuous on the open set $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and integrable there against $\psi$). Consequently the potentials are the smooth functions $$\varphi:=\frac{C}{D}=\frac{C}{\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R,\qquad A:=\frac{\beta\,\varphi}{c}=\frac{\beta\,C}{c\,\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R^3$$ off the worldline, and the distribution $\Phi$ is the regular distribution of $\varphi$, $\Upsilon$ that of $A$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function|regular distribution]]). (c) Let $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]). after.title: Retarded Liénard-Wiechert potentials and fields of a uniformly subluminal smooth point source
after.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, $q\in\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, put $\mu_0:=(c^2\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ and $C:=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*<c$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Write $\Omega:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and $\Gamma:=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}\subseteq\Omega$. For $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ let $s=s(x,t)$ be the unique retarded root of [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]] with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and put $R:=x-z(s)$, $r:=|R|>0$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s)/c$, $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$, $N:=n\cdot\beta$, $D:=\kappa r$, $\dot\beta:=z''(s)/c$ and $d:=n\cdot\dot\beta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then: (a) the distributions $\rho,J\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]], $$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad \langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)\,\psi(z(s),s)\,ds,$$ satisfy $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. (b) Let $K$ be the retarded wave kernel of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] and, for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and $\tau\in\mathbb R$, $y\in\mathbb R^3$, put $(K\circledast\psi)(y,\tau):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,\tau+\cdot)\rangle$. Define the retarded-history pairings by the explicit integrals
$$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle:=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R}(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad
\langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle:=\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds.$$
Here the second integral is componentwise. The notation $\varepsilon_0^{-1}\langle\rho,K\circledast\psi\rangle$ and $\mu_0\langle J,K\circledast\psi\rangle$, if used, means precisely these explicit history integrals, rather than ordinary distribution action on a compactly supported test. These pairings define distributions on $\Omega$, are finite for every $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and satisfy the exact retarded-convolution identities $$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{\beta(x,t)}{c}\,\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt$$ (for $\Upsilon$, componentwise against $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$; both integrands are continuous on the open set $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and integrable there against $\psi$). Consequently the potentials are the $C^2$ functions $$\varphi:=\frac{C}{D}=\frac{C}{\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R,\qquad A:=\frac{\beta\,\varphi}{c}=\frac{\beta\,C}{c\,\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R^3$$ off the worldline, and the zero extensions $\widetilde\varphi,\widetilde A$ on $\Gamma$ belong to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$; $\Phi$ is the regular distribution of $\widetilde\varphi$, and $\Upsilon$ that of $\widetilde A$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function|regular distribution]]). (c) Let $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]). Then, off the worldline, $$E=C\left[\frac{(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)}{\kappa^3r^2}+\frac{n\times\bigl((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta\bigr)}{c\,\kappa^3r}\right],\qquad B=\frac{n\times E}{c}.$$ The fields $E,B$ are $C^1$ off the worldline. More generally, if $z\in C^k$, $k\ge3$, the retarded root is $C^k$, the potentials are $C^{k-1}$ and the fields are $C^{k-2}$ there; if $z\in C^\infty$, all these objects are smooth off the worldline. The result is a mathematical model computation for the stipulated uniformly subluminal smooth worldline and the retarded choice; no self-force law, no radiation-reaction postulate and no physical Maxwell coupling is asserted or proved.
after.strategy:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as stipulated in the statement. (a) Apply [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]] to the $C^1$ curve $z$ on $\mathbb R$; $C^3$ is a special case, and its all-time graph is proper because a compact ambient set bounds the time coordinate.
(b) Fix a compact observation set $Q\subseteq\{(x,t):|x|\le M,\ t_0\le t\le t_1\}$, and tests supported in $Q$. If $g(s,y):=(z(s)+y,s+|y|/c)\in Q$, then $s\le t_1$. For $s\le0$, using $|z(s)|\le Z+v_*|s|$ with $Z:=|z(0)|$ gives
$$t_0\le s+|y|/c=s+|x-z(s)|/c\le -(1-v_*/c)|s|+(M+Z)/c.$$
Thus $s\ge-S$, where $S:=\max\{0,(M+Z-ct_0)/(c-v_*)\}$. If $[-S,t_1]$ is empty no contributing point exists. Otherwise set $H:=\max(S,|t_1|)$ and $L:=1+M+Z+v_*H$. Every contributing $y$ has $|y|\le M+|z(s)|<L$. Consequently the pulled-back support lies in the bounded closed cylinder $[-S,t_1]\times\overline B_L$, possibly approaching $y=0$; it need not be compact inside $U:=\mathbb R\times(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$.
On that cylinder, $|\psi(g(s,y))|/(4\pi|y|)\le\|\psi\|_\infty/(4\pi|y|)$. The polar formula [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] gives $\int_{B_L}|y|^{-1}dy=\sigma(S^2)L^2/2<\infty$. Borel product identification [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]] and the Euclidean/product-measure bridge [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] allow [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] for the absolute value. Then [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] identifies the double integral with the explicit iterated history integral. In particular, with $T:=\max(0,t_1+S)$ and $M_Q:=T\sigma(S^2)L^2/(8\pi)$,
$$|\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle|\le |q|M_Q\|\psi\|_\infty/\varepsilon_0,\qquad
|\langle\Upsilon_j,\psi\rangle|\le\mu_0|q|v_*M_Q\|\psi\|_\infty.$$
The seminorm $\psi\mapsto|\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle|$ restricts continuously to each fixed-support test space by these bounds, and likewise for each component of $\Upsilon$. Thus [[def-test-function-topology]] and [[def-distribution]] prove distribution continuity directly; no action of $\rho$ or $J$ on a noncompact test is assumed.
The graph $\Gamma$ is closed: convergence of $(z(s_j),s_j)$ forces $s_j\to t$ and $z(s_j)\to z(t)$. Thus $V:=\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ is open. On $U$, $g$ is $C^1$, and in coordinate order $(s,y_1,y_2,y_3)$ its determinant is $-\kappa(s,y)$, with $\kappa=1-(y/|y|)\cdot z'(s)/c\ge1-v_*/c>0$. If $g(s,y)=g(s',y')$, then $|s-s'|=||y'|-|y||/c\le|z(s')-z(s)|/c\le(v_*/c)|s-s'|$, so $s=s'$ and $y=y'$. No image point belongs to $\Gamma$: otherwise $|y|=|z(t)-z(s)|\le v_*(t-s)=v_*|y|/c$, contradicting $y\ne0$. Conversely every point of $V$ has the unique retarded root supplied by [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]], giving inverse $(x,t)\mapsto(s(x,t),x-z(s(x,t)))$. Its $C^1$ regularity follows from that supplier's $C^3$ branch on the open domain $x\ne z(t)$, using this consumer's $C^3$ hypothesis. No exclusion of the entire spatial trajectory is imposed. Therefore $g:U\to V$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism.
For any compact $Q\subseteq\Omega$, the nonnegative Borel substitution lemma [[lem-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-borel-functions-via-radon-uniqueness]] applied to $1_Q/(\kappa r)$ on $V$ yields
$$\int_V\frac{1_Q}{\kappa r}\,dx\,dt=\int_U\frac{1_Q(g(s,y))}{|y|}\,ds\,dy<\infty.$$
The same bound holds for $|\beta|/(c\kappa r)$ since $|\beta|\le v_*/c$. Extend the potentials by zero on the closed graph. These extensions are Borel and locally integrable on all of $\Omega$. Applying the same Borel substitution first to the absolute value of $\psi/(\kappa r)$ establishes its $L^1$ integrability on $V$, and [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]] then gives the scalar pairing formula in the statement. Apply it componentwise to $z'(s)$-weighted data for the vector formula. Its prefactor is
$$\frac{\mu_0qz'(s)}{4\pi\kappa r}=\frac{\mu_0qc\beta}{4\pi\kappa r}=\frac{\mu_0c\varepsilon_0 C\beta}{\kappa r}=\frac{C\beta}{c\kappa r},$$
since $\mu_0c^2\varepsilon_0=1$. The regular-distribution identities mean the zero extensions, as in [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]; tests may be nonzero on $\Gamma$. The retarded root is $C^3$ on $V$, and $r,n$ are $C^3$ while $\beta,\kappa,D$ are $C^2$ with $D>0$, so the potentials are $C^2$. The same composition argument gives the matching $C^k$ and $C^\infty$ branches.
(c) Derivatives of the retarded data: from $t-s=r/c$ and R1, $\nabla s=-n/(c\kappa)$, $s_t=1/\kappa$, hence $\nabla r=n/\kappa$ and $r_t=-cN/\kappa$ (chain rule, [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]); $R=x-z(s)$ gives $\partial_iR=e_i+\beta\,n_i/\kappa$ and $\beta=z'(s)/c$ gives $\partial_i\beta=-\dot\beta\,n_i/(c\kappa)$, while $\beta_t=\dot\beta/\kappa$ (componentwise chain rule and [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]). Since $D=r-R\cdot\beta$, the product rules for the Euclidean pairing give $D_t=r_t-R_t\cdot\beta-R\cdot\beta_t=(c(|\beta|^2-N)-rd)/\kappa$ and $\partial_iD=\partial_ir-(\partial_iR)\cdot\beta-R\cdot\partial_i\beta$, hence $\nabla D=((1-|\beta|^2+rd/c)/\kappa)\,n-\beta$; the required product rules are the coordinatewise one-variable product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then $\varphi=C/D$ gives $\nabla\varphi=-C\nabla D/D^2$, $\varphi_t=-CD_t/D^2$, and $A=\beta\varphi/c$ gives $A_t=(\beta_t\varphi+\beta\varphi_t)/c=\dot\beta C/(c\kappa D)-\beta CD_t/(cD^2)$, so $$E=-\nabla\varphi-A_t=\frac{C}{D^2}\Bigl(\nabla D+\frac{\beta D_t}{c}\Bigr)-\frac{C\dot\beta}{c\kappa D}.$$ The bracket equals $\frac{(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)+(rd/c)(n-\beta)}{\kappa}$ (substituting the two displayed identities and $\kappa=1-N$), and writing the second term over the common denominator $\kappa^3r^2$ replaces its numerator by $-r\kappa\dot\beta/c$, giving $E=\frac{C}{\kappa^3r^2}\bigl[(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)+\frac{r}{c}\bigl(d(n-\beta)-\kappa\dot\beta\bigr)\bigr]$; the coordinate triple-product identity $n\times((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta)=d(n-\beta)-\kappa\dot\beta$ (expand both sides with [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]) yields the displayed $E$. For the magnetic field, $\operatorname{curl}(\beta\varphi/c)=\nabla(\varphi/c)\times\beta+(\varphi/c)\operatorname{curl}\beta$ ([[lem-divergence-and-curl-are-linear-and-obey-the-scalar-product-rules]]), and $\operatorname{curl}\beta=\nabla s\times\dot\beta$ by the coordinate formula applied to $\beta=z'(s(x,t))/c$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]); substituting $\nabla\varphi=-C\nabla D/D^2$ and $\nabla s=-n/(c\kappa)$ gives $$B=-C\left[\frac{1-|\beta|^2+rd/c}{c\kappa D^2}\,n\times\beta+\frac{n\times\dot\beta}{c^2\kappa D}\right].$$ Crossing the displayed $E$ with $n/c$ gives this same expression by $n\times(n-\beta)=-n\times\beta$ and $D=\kappa r$, proving $B=n\times E/c$. Both displayed fields are $C^1$ off the worldline, and no derivative of $z$ beyond the third order and no bound on $\Gamma$ at infinity is used; the caveats in the statement are exactly those of the research branch argument.

before.statement: (i) Static specialization. Take $z\equiv0$ (so $v_*=0$), $q\in\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, in the setting of [[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]]. Then for $x\ne0$ the root is $s=t-|x|/c$, $r=|x|$, $n=x/|x|$, $\beta=0$, $\kappa=1$, $\dot\beta=0$, so the potentials and fields are $\varphi=C/|x|$, $A=0$, $E=C\,x/|x|^3$, $B=0$. Thus the retarded formulas reduce exactly to the Coulomb field with the convention $C=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and the kernel identity of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]](b) reproduces the time-independent Poisson kernel $1/(4\pi|x-y|)$ on the static branch: the retarded time is $t-|x-y|/c$ and the $t$-integration of a static $h$ against $\delta(t-s-|x-y|/c)$ selects $s=t-|x-y|/c$. (ii) Explicit Lorenz-gauge transformation. On $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ take $\varphi\equiv0$ and $A(x,t)=(x_1,0,0)$. Then $G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A=1$ and $E=-\partial_tA=0$, $B=\operatorname{curl}A=0$. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), used through the change-of-variables corollaries inside the proof of the retarded-convolution identity cited in clause (b) ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, let $v_*<c$, let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon_0>0$, put $\mu_0:=(c^2\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ and $C:=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and write $\Omega:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and $\Gamma:=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}$.

(a) [Root and emission-time Jacobian] For every $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ (equivalently $x\ne z(t)$) there is exactly one $s=s(x,t)<t$ with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$. The map $s:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^3$, and with $R:=x-z(s)$, $r:=|R|$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s)/c$ and $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) one has $$\partial_ts(x,t)=\kappa^{-1},\qquad \nabla_xs(x,t)=-\frac{n}{c\,\kappa},\qquad \kappa\in[1-v_*/c,\,1+v_*/c],$$ so $\kappa\ge 1-v_*/c>0$ uniformly on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$. Moreover, for the fixed $x$ and near the root, the function $s'\mapsto s'+|x-z(s')|/c$ is differentiable at $s'=s$ with derivative $\kappa(x,t)$: this emission-time Jacobian $1-n\cdot\beta$ is the denominator produced by the delta substitution of clause (b).

Then these pairings are finite for every $\psi$ and their exact retarded-convolution values are $$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{C\,\psi}{\kappa\,r}\,dx\,dt,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{\beta}{c}\,\frac{C\,\psi}{\kappa\,r}\,dx\,dt$$ (the second identity componentwise); equivalently, $\Phi$ and $\Upsilon$ are the regular distributions of the $C^2$ functions $\varphi:=C/(\kappa r)$ and $A:=\beta\varphi/c$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$. The weight $(\kappa r)^{-1}$ with $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$ is the exact form of the substitution with denominator $1-n\cdot\beta$ (the rigorous statement is the displayed pairing identity; composition of $\delta$ with a function is not part of the distribution calculus used here).

(c) [Fields and the velocity/acceleration split] With $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]), and writing $\dot\beta:=z''(s)/c$ at the root, $$E=E_{\mathrm{vel}}+E_{\mathrm{acc}},\qquad E_{\mathrm{vel}}=\frac{C(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)}{\kappa^3r^2},\qquad E_{\mathrm{acc}}=\frac{C\,n\times\bigl((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta\bigr)}{c\,\kappa^3r},\qquad B=\frac{n\times E}{c}$$ at every event of $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]). Both $E$ and $B$ are continuous on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$, and the velocity field obeys the bound $$|E_{\mathrm{vel}}(x,t)|\le C\,\frac{1+v_*/c}{(1-v_*/c)^3}\,r(x,t)^{-2}$$ at every event.

(d) [Uniform far-zone remainder] For every $s_0\in\mathbb R$ and every $n\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|n|=1$, put $x_r:=z(s_0)+rn$ and $t_r:=s_0+r/c$ for $r>0$, and set $\beta_0:=z'(s_0)/c$, $\dot\beta_0:=z''(s_0)/c$, $\kappa_0:=1-n\cdot\beta_0$. Then $(x_r,t_r)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and $s(x_r,t_r)=s_0$ for every $r>0$, and $$E(x_r,t_r)=\frac{C\,n\times\bigl((n-\beta_0)\times\dot\beta_0\bigr)}{c\,\kappa_0^3\,r}+\rho_E(s_0,n,r),\qquad B(x_r,t_r)=\frac{n\times E(x_r,t_r)}{c},$$ where the remainder is bounded uniformly in the direction, $$|\rho_E(s_0,n,r)|\le C\,\frac{1+v_*/c}{(1-v_*/c)^3}\,r^{-2}\qquad\text{for every }n\in S^2\text{ and every }r>0.$$ Equivalently, $rE(x_r,t_r)\to C\,n\times((n-\beta_0)\times\dot\beta_0)/(c\,\kappa_0^3)$ as $r\to\infty$, uniformly over $n\in S^2$ at the explicit rate $O(r^{-1})$ given by the same bound multiplied by $r$. (i) [Plane-wave solutions with infinite spatial $L^2$ norm] Let $c>0$ and $W:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ as in [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. before.statement: Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) and let I be an order-convex subset of R with at least two elements (def-interval); a curve of the model is a map x: I -> A. (a) Derivative and regularity of the parametrization. For s in I and h nonzero with s + h in I the difference quotient (x(s+h) - x(s))/h is an element of V, the displacement from x(s) to x(s+h) divided by the real number h; the curve is differentiable at s when the limit of these quotients as h -> 0 exists in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, and then this limit, written x'(s) in V, is the tangent vector of x at s. If x_A: A -> R^4 is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x is differentiable at s exactly when the R^4-valued map x_A o x is differentiable at s in the sense of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral, and then x'(s) = E((x_A o x)'(s)), where E: R^4 -> V is the frame isomorphism; this does not depend on the inertial chart used, because inertial chart transitions are affine, hence smooth (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas), and all norms on the finite-dimensional V give the same limit. The curve is C^1 when it is differentiable at every point of I and the derivative map s |-> x'(s), I -> V, is continuous (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity); it is C^k for k >= 1 when x' is C^{k-1}. A curve on a compact interval [a,b] contained in I is piecewise C^1 when there is a finite partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b such that x is C^1 on every open subinterval (s_{i-1},s_i) and the one-sided derivatives at the s_i exist; derivatives at the endpoints of I are the one-sided limits over I. (b) Causal character. Let x be differentiable at s in I. Then x is regular at s if x'(s) is not the zero vector; x is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) at s if the vector x'(s) is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) in the sense of def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, and x is future-directed at s if x'(s) is future timelike or future null in the sense of def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets. The zero vector has no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at s. (c) Worldlines. A future timelike worldline (massive worldline) is a C^1 curve x: I -> A with x'(s) future timelike for every s in I; a future causal curve (respectively a future null curve) is a C^1 curve with x'(s) future causal (respectively future null) for every s in I. A piecewise C^1 worldline is a piecewise C^1 curve all of whose one-sided tangents are future timelike, and a C^k worldline is a worldline whose parametrization is C^k; C^2 regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of this page available. The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve s |-> x(-s), which is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by an explicit formula.
before.strategy: A definition item: it fixes the curve, regularity and causal-character language on which the page's items rest, and makes no proof claim beyond well-definedness. Obligations: (i) the difference quotient is an element of V because the affine action gives a displacement for every ordered pair of events, and the limit is taken in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, so no norm has to be chosen; (ii) the identification with the coordinate calculus and the independence of x'(s) and of C^k from the inertial chart are justified by the affine, hence smooth, chart transitions of lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas, with the published vector-valued derivative of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral as the coordinate calculus; (iii) continuity of x' is continuity of a V-valued map (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity), and one-sided derivatives at endpoints are limits over the domain I as in def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral; (iv) causal character and the future/past alternative are those of the model's vector classification and time orientation, with the zero vector excluded, so regularity is implicit in every causal character; (v) null and spacelike curves are distinguished from massive worldlines and are used later only to delimit the proper-time construction. No choice principle is used: all objects are finite-dimensional or explicitly parametrized.

before.title: Total proper time of a piecewise C^1 future timelike worldline
before.statement: Let c > 0 be the conversion constant of def-sr-proper-time and let x: [a,b] -> A be a future timelike worldline with a < b that is piecewise C^1 with partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b (def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline). Corner hypothesis (H): for every i = 1,...,m the derivative s |-> x'(s) of the open piece (s_{i-1},s_i) has finite one-sided limits at s_{i-1} and s_i in V; assigning those limits as endpoint values turns x' into a continuous V-valued map x'_i on the closed piece [s_{i-1},s_i]. Assume (H). Then: (i) for every i the real function g_i(t) := sqrt(-eta(x'_i(t), x'_i(t))) is continuous and strictly positive on [s_{i-1},s_i], hence Riemann integrable there (thm-continuous-implies-integrable); (ii) the total proper time of x from a to b is Delta tau(x) := c^{-1} sum_{i=1}^{m} integral_{s_{i-1}}^{s_i} g_i(t) dt; (iii) the value does not depend on the partition: every refinement of a partition satisfying (H) again satisfies (H) and gives the same sum by additivity of the integral over subintervals, and for any two partitions satisfying (H) the common refinement is a refinement of both, so the sums agree; (iv) if x is C^1 on [a,b] then (H) holds with the single piece [a,b] and Delta tau(x) = tau(b) - tau(a), the proper-time difference of def-sr-proper-time, so the two definitions agree; (v) Delta tau(x) > 0; for a piecewise inertial worldline (def-sr-inertial-and-piecewise-inertial-worldline) Delta tau(x) is the sum over the pieces of the straight-segment proper times c^{-1}(s_i - s_{i-1}) sqrt(-eta(d_i,d_i)); (vi) additivity over concatenation: if additionally a < b < d and x is a future timelike worldline on [a,d] that is piecewise C^1 with a partition having b as a partition point and satisfies (H) for that partition, then for the two restrictions x_1 := x restricted to [a,b] and x_2 := x restricted to [b,d] (each satisfying (H) for the induced partition) one has Delta tau_{[a,d]}(x) = Delta tau_{[a,b]}(x_1) + Delta tau_{[b,d]}(x_2). The item defines the integral only; the reading of an ideal clock along such a history is the separate clock hypothesis of post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light and post-sr-free-trajectories-and-clock-hypothesis.
before.strategy: A definition item with well-definedness obligations. (i) Continuity of g_i: x'_i is continuous and V-valued, eta is bilinear and nondegenerate (def-lorentz-form-and-inertia), so in an eta-orthonormal basis (lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis) t |-> eta(x'_i(t),x'_i(t)) is a finite sum of products of continuous real functions (thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions); the square root is continuous on the positive reals (thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives, def-rational-power, thm-composition-of-continuous-functions). Strict positivity is the future timelike hypothesis on the tangents of the piece (including the one-sided values, which are future timelike because a piecewise C^1 worldline of def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline has future timelike one-sided tangents). Integrability is thm-continuous-implies-integrable for real-valued functions on a compact interval; the oriented convention is that of def-oriented-integral. (ii)-(iii) Partition independence: a refinement of an (H)-partition inherits (H), and thm-additivity-over-subintervals splits each piece integral; the common-refinement argument is then immediate. (iv) With m = 1 and x C^1 on [a,b], (H) holds because a C^1 derivative is continuous on [a,b] with its one-sided endpoint values; the integral is that of def-sr-proper-time. (v) For a piecewise inertial worldline the extended derivative on a piece is the constant d_i, so each piece integral is (s_i - s_{i-1}) times c^{-1} sqrt(-eta(d_i,d_i)), the straight-segment value of def-sr-proper-time. (vi) Concatenation: the induced partitions make the sum over the pieces of x the sum of the two sums. No choice principle is used; all integrals are Riemann integrals of continuous functions on compact intervals.

after.title: Total proper time of a piecewise C^1 future timelike worldline
after.statement: Let c>0 be the conversion constant of def-sr-proper-time and let x:[a,b]->A, a<b, be a piecewise C^1 future timelike worldline in the weak sense of def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline: x is C^1 on each open piece of a finite partition a=s_0<...<s_m=b, its interior tangents and finite one-sided difference-quotient endpoint tangents are future timelike, and continuous extension of the derivative is not assumed. (i) On each open piece let g_i(t)=sqrt(-eta(x'(t),x'(t)))>0. Define its two-ended improper Riemann integral by the convention of lem-sr-weak-piecewise-causal-integrability. That lemma proves each value finite and nonnegative; it is positive since g_i is positive and continuous on a compact interior subinterval. (ii) Define total proper time by Delta tau_[a,b](x)=c^{-1} sum_i integral_(s_(i-1),s_i) g_i. The finite sum is independent of the partition, by subdivision additivity and a common refinement. It is independent of the inertial chart because eta and the tangent are chart independent; constant Lorentz changes preserve the density already on each proper truncation. (iii) Define the based proper-time function tau_x(s)=Delta tau_[s0,s](x) for s>=s0, and tau_x(s)=-Delta tau_[s,s0](x) for s<s0, with tau_x(s0)=0, using restrictions and oriented limits. It is strictly increasing, and changing s0 changes only an additive constant. (iv) Corner hypothesis (H) is the special case in which each open-piece derivative has finite limits at both ends and thus extends continuously to the closed piece. Those limits equal the one-sided quotient derivatives. Under (H), each g_i extends continuously and positively to the closed piece, its improper integral equals its ordinary Riemann integral there, and the same finite-sum formula applies. In particular if x is globally C^1 on [a,b], Delta tau(x)=tau(b)-tau(a) of def-sr-proper-time. (v) Delta tau(x)>0. If on piece i the tangent is a constant future timelike vector d_i, the contribution is c^{-1}(s_i-s_(i-1))sqrt(-eta(d_i,d_i)); this gives the finite sum of straight-segment proper times. (vi) Additivity over concatenation: for a<b<d, restrictions of a weak piecewise worldline x on [a,d] satisfy Delta tau_[a,d](x)=Delta tau_[a,b](x)+Delta tau_[b,d](x). Insert b in the partition and use (ii). The definition supplies metric time only; identification with an ideal clock reading is the separate physical clock postulate. No global C^1 inverse, tangent at a kink, or four-acceleration at a kink is asserted.
after.strategy: Well-definedness is lem-sr-weak-piecewise-causal-integrability: endpoint continuity, finite improper integrals dominated in an inertial chart by the nonnegative time derivative, truncated FTC and partition independence. Strict positivity follows by a compact interior neighborhood on which g_i is positive and continuous. Refinements split each integral, and a common refinement gives independence of the finite partition. Restriction/additivity also give the based function, strict increase and base-point constants. Under (H), if the extended derivative is f_i, truncated FTC gives x(v)-x(u)=integral_u^v f_i. Passing u to the endpoint shows that the one-sided difference quotient is the average of f_i over a shrinking interval and therefore tends to its continuous endpoint value; thus the extension equals the finite quotient tangent. The extended density is continuous and strictly positive on the compact closed piece. Its bounded omitted endpoint tails tend to zero, so its improper value equals the ordinary Riemann value. Global C1 is the one-piece (H) case and agrees with def-sr-proper-time. Constant tangents give the displayed straight-segment calculation directly. All steps are finite-dimensional one-variable real analysis and use no choice principle; no physical premise supplies mathematical integrability.

before.title: Adopted free trajectories of massive particles and the clock hypothesis
before.statement: Adopt as physical assumptions of this framework, extending the ideal-clock reading rule of post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light to the general worldline calculus of this page: (i) Free trajectories. A massive test particle that is subject to no interaction (a free particle) has as its worldline a straight future timelike line of the affine model: there are an event p in A and a future timelike vector v in V with x(s) = p + (s - s_0) v for all s (the kinematical consequences of this shape for the four-velocity are derived, not assumed, in pthm-sr-four-velocity-norm-and-orthogonality). Interactions, forces and collisions are not part of this assumption: a particle that is not free may have any future timelike worldline admitted by its own dynamical model, and no force law is adopted here. (ii) Clock hypothesis. An ideal clock carried along a future timelike worldline of the model, including an accelerated one and a piecewise C^1 one with finitely many kinks, reads between any two parameter values the proper-time difference of def-sr-proper-time, with no additional term depending on acceleration, jerk or any higher derivative; a kink is an idealization of a finite short acceleration phase whose contribution is included through the integral on the smooth pieces, and the reading does not depend on the choice of the increasing parameter. (iii) Scope and qualification. The assumptions concern ideal point particles, ideal clocks and flat classical spacetime. They are adopted, not proved; they are not consequences of the affine geometry, and no experiment is claimed here to establish them. They inherit the idealizations of post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light: real clocks have finite resolution, calibration and apparatus limitations, and real particles are not exactly free.
before.strategy: A postulate, not a theorem: it fixes the physical interpretation of straight future timelike lines as the histories of free massive test particles and makes the clock-reading rule applicable to the general worldline class of this page. Obligations: (i) straight future timelike lines are declared objects of the affine model, and each is a future timelike worldline with constant tangent (def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline); (ii) the reading rule is an identification of a physical clock reading with the mathematical proper-time difference, so def-sr-proper-time and its reparametrization invariance are the mathematical suppliers carrying the content, while the identification itself is adopted; (iii) the free-trajectory clause is deliberately silent about interactions and force laws, so it cannot be used to infer conservation laws, mass-shell relations or collision kinematics, which require the separate momentum postulate of the later energy-momentum page; (iv) the clock hypothesis is the assertion that ideal clocks have no acceleration-dependent term, so it must not be presented as following from the geometry. No proof is manufactured; the item is an adopted premise with an exact scope.

before.title: A closed 1-form on a simply connected open subset of the affine model has a primitive
before.statement: Let U be a nonempty open subset of A which, with the manifold topology of lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas, is path-connected and simply connected (def-simply-connected), and let alpha be a C^1 one-form on U with d alpha = 0 (def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms). Then there is a C^2 function F: U -> R with dF = alpha. Consequently, for any two piecewise C^1 paths gamma_0, gamma_1 in U with the same endpoints the integrals of alpha along them are equal, and the integral of alpha along every piecewise C^1 loop in U vanishes.

after.title: A closed 1-form on a simply connected open subset of the affine model has a primitive
after.statement: Let U be a nonempty open subset of A which, with the manifold topology of lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas, is path-connected and simply connected (def-simply-connected), and let alpha be a C^1 one-form on U with d alpha = 0 (def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms). Then there is a C^2 function F: U -> R with dF = alpha. Consequently, for any two piecewise C^1 paths gamma_0, gamma_1 in U with the same endpoints the integrals of alpha along them are equal, and the integral of alpha along every piecewise C^1 loop in U vanishes. Here for a C^1 one-form, closedness means in an inertial chart alpha=sum_i a_i dx^i with partial_i a_j=partial_j a_i; the exterior derivative is understood by this coefficient formula. (2) Compact small-cell construction. Uniform continuity of H gives delta>0 such that domain distances less than delta imply image distances less than r/2. Choose a finite rectangular mesh with cell diameter less than delta. For each cell, its lower-left image vertex belongs to a half-radius ball; the entire cell image is therefore contained in the corresponding full-radius ball. before.title: Counterexample: a Born-rigid congruence need not be a Killing congruence
before.statement: Statement refuted: 'every smooth Born-rigid future unit timelike field n is locally a positive multiple of a Killing field'.
